chunks: Motor vs solenoid. The question: What is the difference between a motor and solenoid?
Both motors and solenoids are coils that turn electricity into motion using magnetic force. A motor spins continuously.
A solenoid has a plunger that pulls in a short distance, then stops. Use a motor when you need steady turning and a solenoid when you need a quick push, latch or valve.
A motor is like a ceiling fan: it keeps turning as long as the power is on. A solenoid is like a doorbell hammer or a door latch. It snaps once and holds.
Both are "magnet machines", but one makes a loop of motion and the other makes a single stroke.
The analogy has a limit: a fan runs freely, while a solenoid holding a latch is using power the whole time without moving.
A low-side N-MOSFET switches the coil.
D1 sits across the coil with its cathode on the +12 volts side, so it is reverse-biased while the coil is energised and conducts the coil current when Q1 opens.
A motor drops in where the coil is.
Motor: a coil-and-magnet machine that gives continuous rotation. Solenoid: a coil with an iron plunger that moves a short distance when current flows.
Inductive load: a coil-based load, so it kicks back when switched off. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor makes against the supply.
Flyback diode: a diode across the coil that absorbs the kickback.
Say a 12 volts solenoid coil has 24 ohms of resistance. Once settled, it draws 12 volts / 24 ohms = 0. 5 amps, which is 6 watts.
The plunger moves once, then the coil just sits there turning those 6 watts into heat while it holds.
A 12 volts motor with the same winding would draw less current once it spins, because its back-EMF fights the supply.
That is the whole idea: both are coils, but one is built for continuous rotation and one for a short stroke.
"Both are coils that turn current into mechanical force and both are inductive loads that need flyback protection.
A motor makes continuous rotation with torque proportional to current and a back-EMF that limits its current as it speeds up.
A solenoid pulls an iron plunger in over a short linear stroke: force goes roughly as current squared and rises sharply as the gap closes.
Motors for continuous motion, solenoids for short on/off pushes like valves and latches. Holding a solenoid on costs I to the 2R continuously, so we use peak-and-hold PWM."
